the correlation between predicted and labeled values, and the closer
to 1 demonstrating the higher the correlation between predicted and
labeled values:
MAE, MSE, and RMSE are sensitive to
data, especially abnormal data.
In this case, the Pearson, Kendall, and Spearman correlation coefficients
are alternative choices to evaluate the model performance. These functions
can mitigate the data sensitivity, for instance, the Pearson coefficient
in equation 6, the abnormal
data can enlarge both the numerator and denominator terms, so their
impact on the overall expression is reduced. Besides, the range of
these three correlation coefficients are normalized within (−1,1),
providing a relative uniform interval for model evaluation.89 Grid search can attempt every combination of
hyperparameters for hyperparameters optimization to acquire a suitable
set of configurations although it may take a prolonged time cost,
and Bayesian optimization is one approach searching for the best combination
of parameters.
Model
parameters refer to intrinsic variables within the model that can
be automatically adjusted based on the training data without any manual
intervention. Examples of model parameters include weights in Artificial
Neural Networks (ANN) and support vectors in Support Vector Machines
(SVM). In contrast, hyperparameters are external variables that cannot
be adjusted during the training process and require manual setting.
Examples of hyperparameters include the learning rate, the depth of
hidden layers, and the number of neurons in each layer of an ANN.
Hyperparameters play a crucial role in shaping the behavior of the
model and optimizing its performance. During the training process,
the training set is used to optimize the model parameters, ensuring
that the model fits the training data as accurately as possible. The
validation set is utilized to tune the hyperparameters, finding the
optimal configuration that maximizes the model’s performance
on unseen data. The test set, comprising samples unseen by the model
during training, is employed to evaluate the generalization capability
of the final optimized model. The key distinction between the validation
set and the test set lies in whether the data has been seen by the
model during training. The data in the test set should never be used
before optimizing the model parameters.90 This distinction ensures an unbiased evaluation of the model’s
performance on new and unseen data. It avoids also potential overfitting
and provides a reliable assessment of the model’s generalizability.
Hyperparameter optimization plays a critical role in determining
the final performance of a model. For instance, the choice of learning
rate can significantly impact the convergence speed. Researchers can
select a relatively large learning rate at the initial stage of training
to accelerate the learning process, followed by gradually decreasing
the learning rate until the model converges.91 In deep learning models, various methods are employed to update
or evaluate the learning rate, such as the learning rate annealing
method and the cyclic learning rate.92 When
it comes to model validation and optimization, two widely used techniques
are Hold-out and k-fold cross-validation.93,94 In k-fold cross-validation, the input data is randomly
divided into k equal-sized parts, known as folds.
The first fold is set as the validation data, while the remaining
folds are used as the training set. This process is repeated until
each fold has been used as the validation data, and the k results are then averaged to assess the machine learning performance.
It is essential for the model to exhibit good generalization ability
across the data set to achieve high cross-validation scores consistently.
By effectively optimizing hyperparameters and employing robust validation
methods, the performance and reliability of their ML models can be
enhanced, making them more accurate and efficient in solving the challenges
in complex metamaterial design.
According to how the learning procedure is designed, ML algorithms
can be classified as supervised, unsupervised, semisupervised, and
reinforcement learning, as shown in Figure 2. Supervised and semisupervised learning
are trained totally or partially by the director labels, while unsupervised
and reinforcement are trained without labels. ML discriminative models,
e.g., deep neural networks, can build a structure property mapping
of metamaterials rather than solving partial differential equations.
Therefore, ML serves as a surrogate model to predict the properties
of the metamaterial by replacing the simulations. Because the ML model
can map the design parameters to the response, one may apply the trained
model directly for a brute force sweep over the design space to find
optimal design parameter sets that can generate the desired response.
Furthermore, ML generative models such as Autoencoder, Variational
Autoencoder, Adversarial Autoencoder, and Generative Adversarial Networks
have been developed based on the surrogate models to achieve inverse
design by producing the design parameters for given the required properties.

Classification
of machine learning and their approaches.
Supervised
learning techniques can be broadly categorized into two main types:
classification and regression.42 In classification
problems, each sample is labeled with a specific class, and the supervised
learning algorithm is trained to determine to which class the input
sample most likely belongs. On the other hand, in regression, the
machine learning model produces a predicted real-value number to characterize
the property of the input sample. Regression has found extensive applications
in metamaterials research, as it enables the training of machine learning
models to predict specific properties of metamaterials based on given
parameters. Supervised machine learning encompasses a wide range of
algorithms, including Neural Networks, Random Forests, Decision Trees,
Support Vector Machines, and Bayesian optimization. These algorithms
are widely utilized in metamaterials studies to extract meaningful
patterns and relationships from data, making them valuable tools for
predictive modeling and materials design. Their applications allow
researchers to gain deeper insights into the behavior of metamaterials
and facilitates the discovery of novel materials with desired properties.
In contrast
to supervised learning, unsupervised learning involves training with
label-free data to unveil underlying structures within the input data
by inferring a function automatically. The principal advantage of
unsupervised learning lies in its ability to minimize the efforts
required by researchers to prepare the database, as it operates without
labeling data during the training phase. This attribute proves to
be highly advantageous in scenarios where obtaining labeled data are
needed for sophisticated experimental operations or intensive computations
in simulation. Furthermore, unsupervised learning exhibits the capability
to unveil previously undetected patterns that may have eluded the
notice of experts responsible for data preparation. Unsupervised learning
includes various algorithms, such as clustering, association rule
learning, representation learning, and dimensionality reduction,95 etc.
Clustering is a data mining technique
that groups data with similar characteristics into clusters while
maintaining distinguishable gaps between different clusters.96 Clustering tasks can be achieved automatically
by predefined algorithms, making it a convenient technique for researchers
to use. Commonly used clustering algorithms include k-means, mean shift, and Gaussian mixture model.97,98 For instance, k-means is a clustering algorithm
that categorizes the original data set into a predefined number of k groups based on the distances between each group’s
centroid. However, a key challenge in clustering lies in defining
the different classes partitioned by algorithms in the absence of
manually defined category standards. Therefore, the clustering technique
is best utilized in conjunction with real-world problems, where different
types of materials can serve as standards to assess whether the clustering
task has been executed effectively.
Association rule learning,
on the other hand, identifies correlations
and dependencies among a large number of variables, describing patterns
of simultaneous occurrences.99 Representation
learning involves a method where a model automatically extracts features
or representations from a database.100 This
transformation of raw data into a format that can be effectively operated
by machine learning models allows computers to extract features during
the learning process. Additionally, representation learning mitigates
the burden of manual feature extraction, which provides valuable tools
for understanding the underlying structures of data, finding patterns
in complex data sets, and enabling machines to automatically derive
meaningful features from the raw data, enhancing the overall performance
of machine learning models.
Dimensionality reduction is a fundamental
technique used to transform
data from a feature-rich space into a lower-dimensional space while
retaining its essential characteristics that are intrinsic to the
data properties. The underlying assumption is that these crucial features
are encoded within a low-dimensional manifold, but the data is currently
represented in a high-dimensional space with some superfluous and
irrelevant information. By eliminating the redundant data, linear
or nonlinear dimensionality reduction methods can project the original
data onto a lower-dimensional representation while preserving the
meaningful aspects of the data. These extracted features are then
utilized for machine learning algorithms. Two widely adopted algorithms
are Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and Linear Discriminant Analysis
(LDA).101,102 PCA generates orthogonal features to reduce
or eliminate correlations in the data. It computes a set of orthogonal
vectors, known as principal components, which represent new features
capturing the maximum variance of the data points. Conversely, LDA
is designed to identify orthogonal vectors that maximize the variance
of the data points across different classes. Both PCA and LDA efficiently
reduce the redundant dimensionality of the data; however, they assume
a linear relationship between features and the target property, which
may not always hold true in practical scenarios. To address nonlinear
relationships, several nonlinear projection algorithms have been developed,
such as Isometric Feature Mapping (Isomap), t-distributed Stochastic
Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE), and Uniform Manifold Approximation and
Projection (UMAP). Notably, t-SNE and UMAP have gained popularity
for data visualization and assessing the applicability of machine
learning models on diverse data sets. It is important to note that
some dimensionality reduction techniques may lead to the loss of less
relevant information, potentially resulting in reduced model performance.
Therefore, when applying these methods in practice, careful consideration
and thorough evaluation are necessary to strike a balance between
preserving essential features and mitigating the loss of pertinent
data.
The major
disadvantage of supervised learning is that it requires a high cost
to label the data set manually before training. To resolve this issue,
one may refer to semisupervised learning, which bridges supervised
and unsupervised learning. It utilizes a small portion of labeled
data to train the initial model and then iteratively applies it to
a large number of unlabeled data. Semisupervised learning uses pseudolabeling
to train the model, and the whole workflow is explained as follows.
First, a base model is trained with the help of labeled data which
is the same as ordinary supervised learning. Next, the partially trained
model is used to predict the unlabeled data to generate a pseudo label.
Moreover, adding the pseudolabels with the most confident predictions
into the original labeled database, and improving the model with further
training. Finally, the model’s performance will be increased
after several iterations, with more pseudolabels being added at every
iteration.
Reinforcement
learning constitutes a significant component of the machine learning
field, distinguishing itself from supervised learning, which relies
on labeled input data for training. In reinforcement learning, an
agent is trained to interact with its surrounding environment in pursuit
of maximizing cumulative rewards provided as feedback from the environment,
as shown in Figure 3. During each training iteration, the agent exerts slight change
on the environment, observing the feedback generated by the environment
in response to its actions. These feedback signals can be positive
rewards, meant to encourage desirable actions, or negative punishments,
intended to discourage undesirable behaviors. The agent’s decision-making
process, known as the policy, is shaped through training to discover
a long-term strategy that optimizes the cumulative rewards obtained
over multiple episodes of interaction with the environment.

Schematics
of reinforcement learning.
In the specific context of metamaterial optimization,
the agent’s
actions involve making slight adjustments to the design parameters,
while the environment evaluate the properties and response of the
metamaterial under such adjustments, through simulation or experiments.
If the agent’s policy result in the metamaterial’s properties
approaching the desired value, the feedback is positive and serves
as a reward; otherwise, it becomes a negative punishment. Reinforcement
learning is particularly advantageous in scenarios where a prepared
data set is unavailable, as the agent learns through trial-and-error
exploration. One of the prominent algorithms employed in reinforcement
learning is Q-learning, which utilizes the Q-function to represent
state values and store the rewards achieved after each action.103 Demonstrating the power of these techniques,
the AlphaGo program, developed by DeepMind, serves as a noteworthy
example. AlphaGo achieved a milestone victory over the world champion
in the game of GO in 2016, showcasing the effectiveness of these methodologies
in real-world applications.104
The neural
network is the fundamental supervised learning approach in metamaterials
research. NN is inspired by the structure and function of the human
brain, consisting of artificial neurons that resemble biological neurons,
as shown in Figure 4b. Each artificial neuron, known as a perceptron, receives input
information x = (x1,x2, . . .xn) and computes a weighted sum, which is then processed by an
activation function to produce an output y = σ(∑ni = 1wixi + b), where σ is the activation function applied to
weighted sum ∑ni = 1wixi plus a bias b. The activation function introduces
nonlinearity to the output y, enabling the neural
network to model complex nonlinear functions. When multiple layers
of perceptron are interconnected, they form a multilayer perceptron,
also known as a feed-forward network, as shown in Figure 4a. Consequently, the multilayer
perceptron is capable of approximating intricate nonlinear functions.
A typical structure of a neural network which can be divided into
3 classes of layers: input layer, hidden layer, and output layer.
The basic idea of neural network is that input information propagates
forward, and errors return backward. The terms deep neural network
and artificial neural network are often used interchangeably to refer
to these classic multilayer perceptron models.

(a) Illustration of artificial
neural network. (b) The workflow
of a perception.
Some commonly used activation functions are sigmoid,105 hyperbolic tangent (tanh), rectified linear
unit (ReLU),106 and Leaky Rectified Linear
Unit (Leaky ReLU). Selecting an appropriate activation function is
technical and should consider the realistic physical meaning of metamaterials’
property. The loss function supervises the error between the predicted
output and label to monitor the convergence of training. To obtain
the best prediction, the loss function should be minimized through
the backpropagation algorithm and update the weights and biases by
gradient descent.107 The loss function’s
gradients for weights at each layer are acquired by backpropagating
the gradient calculation result at the end layer using the chain rule.
Loss function can be optimized by several developed optimizers, such
as stochastic gradient decent (SGD) and Adam.108 The weights and biases are changed along with the negative
gradient orientation of the loss function (the fastest decreasing
direction of loss function) to decrease the loss values. Consequently,
the mismatch between prediction and label values is diminished during
training.
Deep
neural network architecture contains deeper hidden layers with more
neurons in each layer. Each hidden layer receives input from the preceding
layer and produces output that is then forwarded to the subsequent
layer. The representations formed in each layer are nonlinear combinations
of the representations from the preceding layer, resulting in hierarchical
feature extraction and abstraction.100 As
a consequence, DNN can learn simple features in the initial layers
and progressively combine them to derive more complex abstractions
in subsequent layers. This characteristic makes DNN well-suited for
predicting intricate mapping relations and handling large volumes
of training data, leading to its popularity in metamaterials research.109 However, the high-dimensional structure of
DNN with multiple hidden layers renders the internal representations
challenging to be interpreted. Consequently, DNN is often referred
to as a “black-box” model, as it becomes difficult to
understand its decision-making logic and comprehend the learned features
and relationships.
Although a deeper neural network can usually
increase prediction accuracy, it does not imply that a deep and complex
neural network structure is preferable in any case. The data set size
and the dimension of deep neural networks are closely related, and
a good match between these two factors can increase the training convergence
speed, enhance prediction accuracy, and facilitate inverse design
for optimal global solutions. Two significant problems usually appear
because of the inappropriate match: overfitting and underfitting.
If the trained model produces high accuracy in the training data set
while failing in the validation set, this is called overfitting. It
is mostly caused by the DNN model is designed as too complicated for
predicting on a relatively simple mapping relation between design
space and response space. Thus, we can simplify the DNN model such
as reducing the number of neurons in each layer, using a smaller number
of hidden layers, and using the dropout method that lets a fraction
of neurons stop working during training. Besides, the deeper hidden
layers may raise two extra problems: gradient vanishing (gradient
values tend to be infinitesimal) and gradient explosion (gradient
tends to infinity). In this case, we may add the residual block (ResNet)
as the shortcut to skip a few hidden layers during dataflow.
On the contrary, if the machine learning model performs poorly
in both the training and validation set, this is usually caused by
insufficient training samples. A smaller data set typically returns
low accuracy for the neural network model due to insufficient representation
of the mapping relation. In this case, preparing more training samples
to increase the data set size is helpful.110 Indeed, some experiments and computational techniques for specific
metamaterial problems can only give small data sets due to complex
experimental methods or high computational costs. This will cause
difficulty in applying the machine learning approach.
The convolutional neural network is one of the commonly used algorithms
in computer vision designed for image analysis, but its capacity to
analyze sequent data has also been explored.111 As shown in Figure 5, CNN contains multiple hidden layers that can be classified into
three categories: Convolutional Layer (conv), Pooling Layer (pooling),
and Fully Connected Layer (FC). Instead of analyzing the entire image
pixel by pixel, the Convolutional Layer can recognize specific patterns
in the image block by block. Specifically, conv uses a set of filters
constituted by m × m dimension
of square matrixes to slide over the entire input image and compute
the dot product between the filter weights with the input pixel values.
Filter weights are optimized during training. Through this, CNN extracts
every local feature at a specific location in the image and outputs
a feature map. Weight sharing can reduce the number of weights that
need to be trained, which save the model training time and cost. The
first conv typically detects low-level features, such as edges and
colors, while added layers extract high-level features. Thus, CNN
can acquire a global understanding of the input data set. The layer
appended to each convolutional layer is the pooling layer, which is
responsible for reducing the feature map’s dimension and preventing
overfitting. There are two commonly used pooling operations: average
pooling and max pooling. The feature map from the previous conv is
divided into several square-shaped regions. Average pooling takes
the average value of each region on the feature map to convert into
a single neuron, while max pooling takes the maximum value of every
region. The third type of layer in CNN is a fully connected neural
network, where each neuron in this layer will be connected to all
the numbers in the previous volume. The performance of neural networks
in computer vision tasks like CNN depends a lot on the training data
set size. To increase the generality and diversity of image data set,
the image data augmentation is typically used to create new images
from the existing data set via a variety of methods. Rotation, reflection,
scaling and distortion are commonly selected to create new images.112 Enlarging the data set can also reduce the
overfitting possibility.

Schematic diagram of Convolutional Neural Network
for classification
on MNIST Database.
Hyperparameter
tuning of deep learning is a key issue, which include the number of
hidden layers, the number of neurons of each layer, the selection
of activation function, learning rate, the number of training epochs
and batch sizes, etc. Adequate combination of these hyperparameters
will train the algorithm efficiently and successfully. However, a
combination of hyperparameters that works well for one specific problem
may perform poorly for another situation. Learning rate (α)
is used to update the weights of the neural network during training.
α is quite sensitive in gradient decent approach especially
in high-dimensional space and multilayer neural networks. If α
is too small, the learning process is slow, and it would take more
time for learning. In contrast, if α is too large, the learning
process would become faster while may miss the optimal solution point.
Basically, α should not be kept as a constant value throughout
learning. Based on the evaluation results of machine learning model,
the hyperparameters can be tuned by grid search and random search.113
Generative models
have the capability to learn and capture the distribution of high-dimensional
data, subsequently compressing them into a reduced-dimensional space
known as the latent space. By sampling points in the latent space,
generative models can generate various data points that are “similar”
to those present in the training set. This transformation to a new
representation implies that the original locally optimal solutions
in the design parameter space might also change or even disappear
in the compact latent space. Consequently, the globally optimal design
can be identified by thoroughly exploring the compact representation.
Furthermore, the dimensionality reduction property of generative
models offers valuable insights into the relationships among training
data sets, facilitating the optimization process. This understanding
of data relationships aids in efficiently finding optimal solutions
and avoiding local minima during the optimization procedure. By combining
generative networks with optimization algorithms, designers can benefit
from an effective approach to design exploration, taking advantage
of both the generative capabilities and optimization techniques for
enhanced efficiency and avoiding local minima.
Goodfellow introduced the Generative Adversarial Network in 2014
as one of the most popular generative models.800 GAN is composed of two neural networks, a generator network G and a discriminator network D. The generator G generates fake images, and the discriminator D evaluates the authenticity. The two networks compete with each other
in every training step; ultimately, the competition leads to mutual
improvement of each network, so that G can generate
higher-quality realistic images. The generator creates an image from
a noise vector and proposes this image to the discriminator. The discriminator
works as a classification network and learns to decide whether the
image sample it received is from the data set or proposed by the generator.
Suppose the discriminator recognizes that the received image is fake,
the proposed sample will be rejected. On the contrary, the generator
learns to generate an image that is as authentic as possible to fool
the discriminator. Two modules are becoming stronger and stronger
in training. The training process terminates when the classification
accuracy of the discriminator attains 0.5, which indicates that the
discriminator can no longer distinguish between the fake and real
image because the two networks are at Nash equilibrium. In the metamaterial
design problem, the input noise for the generator can be combined
with the realistic metamaterial’s response vector (e.g., optical
spectrum) to generate the image pattern. Therefore, the generator
is encoded with response space to produce the design pattern under
the required response control. A representation of the architecture
of the GAN is presented in Figure 6. GAN is difficult to train because there are two dependent
neural networks to be optimized at the same time.

Structure of Generative
Adversarial Networks (GAN)
GAN is limited in its ability to generate samples
only within the
range of the training data. In the context of inverse design problems,
where we aim to create samples with specific desired properties, a
variant of the GAN model called the Conditional Generative Adversarial
Network (CGAN) has been developed to address this limitation.114 To tackle the inverse design problem, we include
the desired material’s response as the conditioning information,
which is combined with the random noise and then input into the generator.
This allows the CGAN to generate samples that meet the specific requirements
specified by the conditions. The training process of CGAN is similar
to that of the conventional GAN model. CGAN is, therefore, an elegant
and effective approach to address material inverse design challenges,
offering the potential to produce tailored materials with desired
properties.
To
understand the origin of many-to-one problem that exists in inverse
design, let us consider a specific metamaterial with a set of design
parameters denoted by , and the objective is to search for the
optimal parameter combinations to achieve a desired response denoted
by . Initially, a forward neural network can
be trained for property prediction, taking the structural parameters
as input and generating predictions of the response properties as
output. For inverse design, a common approach is to train an inverse
neural network that maps the input response  to the output design parameters . Consequently, the inverse network is expected
to generate design parameters corresponding to a given required response.
However, this process can lead to the generation of different design
spaces  and  corresponding to the same input response , which we refer to as a “many-to-one”
problem. This nonunique mapping from  to  creates a one-to-many relationship between
the inputs and outputs of the inverse network. As a consequence, the
inverse network becomes challenging to train, as the one-to-many relationship
introduces conflicting optimization objectives during the neural network
training process. The backpropagation algorithm is uncertain about
whether it should update the weights of the inverse network to minimize
the loss relative to one ground truth design parameter set  or another . This situation renders the inverse network
generally untrainable.
The nonuniqueness problem has been effectively
addressed by the Tandem Neural Network (TNN), as introduced by Liu
et al.44 in 2018. The objective is to design
the thickness of each layer in a thin film composed of alternating
SiO2 and Si3N4 layers to achieve
a desired transmission spectrum. As shown in Figure 7, The TNN consists of two interconnected
neural networks: a pretrained forward neural network and an inverse
network. The forward network is initially trained to predict the response
space  based on the input design space . Once the connection between these two
networks is established, the entire TNN is jointly trained. To train
the entire TNN, the response space  is inputted at first. The inverse network
then generates the design space at an intermediate layer, commonly
referred to as the bottleneck layer. Subsequently, the proposed design
parameters are passed through the pretrained forward network to obtain
the corresponding response. During the joint training process, the
weights and biases within the forward network remain unchanged, while
the weights and biases of the hidden layers in the inverse network
are optimized by minimizing the difference between the input response
space and the response predicted by the forward network. To achieve
the inverse design task, the required response acts as the input,
and the candidate design structures are obtained from the intermediate
layer. Because each structure corresponds to a unique response, the
inverse design becomes a one-to-one problem, effectively resolving
the issue of nonuniqueness problem.

Construction of Tandem network.
Empowered by
the Tandem structure, the Autoencoder has found extensive application
in the inverse design of materials problems. An autoencoder is a type
of neural network that learns to compress and encode data in a reduced-dimensional
representation, and subsequently, reconstructs the data from this
compressed representation back to a form that faithfully resembles
the original input. A typical framework of autoencoder is illustrated
in Figure 8. The autoencoder
architecture comprises three main parts: an encoder, which reduces
the dimensionality of the input data; a bottleneck layer (latent space)
that represents the reduced representation of the input data; and
a decoder, which expands the compressed representation to reconstruct
the variables at the output and match the original input. During training,
the weights of autoencoder are updated by minimizing the distance
between the original and reconstructed data. By performing this process
iteratively, the autoencoder learns to capture the essential features
of the input data in the latent space. Autoencoder finds utility in
dimensionality reduction of both the design space and response space,
enabling a better understanding of the underlying relationships and
representations within the data.110,115,116

Architecture of Autoencoder (AE) network.
VAE was first introduced in 2013 and has the capability to learn
geometrical features of metamaterial structures and reconstruct various
representations of these features by sampling from a latent-variable
distribution.117 In the architecture of
VAE shown in Figure 9, the encoder does not map the input data directly to points in the
latent space, but instead, it maps them to probability distributions.
These distributions vary according to the input data and are modeled
as Gaussian distributions with mean and covariance matrix values.
Therefore, the encoder outputs the mean and covariance matrix of the
latent-space distributions. The decoder functions as a generative
network, utilizing the latent-space distributions to generate data
distributions. The encoder and decoder frameworks can be tailored
to the particular problem at hand.

Variational Autoencoder (VAE) network
architecture.
The loss function of the VAE consists of two components:
the reconstruction
loss and the regularization loss. The reconstruction loss is similar
to that of an autoencoder and quantifies the difference between the
input and the reconstructed structure. A smaller reconstruction loss
indicates better data reconstruction. The regularization loss, on
the other hand, evaluates the discrepancy between the output multivariate
Gaussian distribution from the encoder and a standard multivariate
distribution. A smaller regularization loss indicates a more accurate
projection. By combining these loss functions, the VAE can generate
diverse samples and facilitates the exploration and optimization of
metamaterial designs.
As shown in Figure 10, AAE consists of three components: the encoder, the decoder/generator,
and the discriminator. Like the VAE, the encoder compresses input
patterns into a compact, continuous latent space. The decoder learns
to reconstruct real-space patterns based on the coordinates in the
latent space, known as latent vectors. However, unlike VAE, where
the latent space distribution assumes a standard normal distribution,
AAE employs an adversarial learning approach similar to GAN. In this
approach, the discriminator is utilized to map the latent space to
a predefined model distribution, resulting in AAE combining the functionalities
of both VAE and GAN.

Architecture of Adversarial Autoencoder (AAE).
AAE possesses three advantages over other deep
generative architectures,
such as VAE and GAN. First, AAE provides the neural network with a
dense and continuous latent space representation,118 which is essential for effectively interpolating the hyper-dimensional
parametric space. This continuous representation significantly expands
the design space of metamaterial structures, enabling a wider range
of generated possibilities. Second, AAE offers great flexibility in
controlling the configuration of the latent space, as it does not
impose specific limitations on a predefined model distribution. This
allows for more freedom in shaping the latent space to suit specific
design requirements. Finally, AAE networks demonstrate better trainability
compared to GAN. This improved trainability arises from the discriminator
in AAE working on a compressed continuous latent representation, while
in GAN, adversarial learning is directly applied to patterns/images,
which can lead to stability issues during training.
Support vector machine is a supervised machine learning algorithm
used for classification and regression in most materials’ science
problems. It is based on statistical learning theory and was described
by Vapnik in 1995. A Support Vector Machine has been applied to predict
the metamaterial antenna bandwidth and gain. In implementing an SVM
algorithm for classification, each data set is plotted as a point
in a dimensional space equal to the number of features. For example,
the goal for a two-class problem is to separate these two clusters
of samples by a line (hyperplane), and two sets of samples are distributed
on the opposite side of this line, as shown in Figure 11. Because there are many possible choices
of the hyperplane, the objective is to find the hyperplane with the
maximal distance between the data points of the two classes. SVM uses
the samples on the edge of the margin to separate samples. It is a
powerful approach to deal with data sets that are not separable by
nonlinear mapping to a higher dimension.119 Finding a hyperplane that has the largest separation between nearest
data optimizes the classification and defines the support vectors.
The high generalization and feasibility for a small data set are two
of its most significant advantages.120

Schematic
diagram representing the fundamental principle of Support
Vector Machine (SVM).
The kNN is a supervised learning algorithm that retains all available
categories and classifies newly added data based on a similarity measure.
The parameter k specifies the number of neighbors
to be examined to determine the classification of a specific query
point. The proximity between a given query point and its neighboring
data points is assessed using distance metrics. Commonly used distance
metrics include Euclidean distance, Manhattan distance, and Minkowski
distance. Assuming k is 5, as illustrated in Figure 12, for a query point P, there are 3 nearest points belonging to class C. Consequently,
point P can be classified as belonging to category
C. kNN is straightforward to comprehend and implement, and it requires
minimal hyperparameter tuning because the main consideration is to
choose an appropriate value for k. However, as all
training data are stored in memory, the algorithm can become considerably
slower with increasing numbers of examples or variables. Moreover,
kNN is susceptible to overfitting issues, which is why dimensionality
reduction techniques are often employed.

Schematics of k nearest neighbor.
The Decision Tree
algorithm takes the input data and uses it as the root of a tree.
It then selects characteristics from the data set to create nodes
(decision points) that divide the data into different subsets. This
process is iteratively repeated until the subsets contain data of
the same type. Figure 13 depicts the flowchart of the decision tree. It begins with a root
node and then branches into different internal nodes based on the
available features. Ultimately, the leaf nodes represent all possible
classifications within the data set. The Decision Tree algorithm is
a suitable choice when there exits an inherent correlation within
the data. However, a significant drawback of this algorithm is its
tendency to overfit the data, which can lead to a poor generalization
on new data.121 To address the overfitting
issue, two submodels have been developed: Random Forest and Gradient
Boosting Decision Tree (GBDT).

Schematics of decision tree.
The Random Forests
algorithm is a supervised machine learning technique that combines
multiple decision trees as an ensemble, and each individual tree in
the random forest proposes a class prediction. Each individual decision
tree is a flowchart-like structure that receives the input data at
its root, then raises a series of logical questions at their internal
nodes associated with the possible answers followed by the branches,
and each leaf node (terminal node) holds the final answer to the series
of questions. Random Forests are also called Ensemble techniques because
they collect each prediction of the decision tree to output the regression
or classification results. A regression problem uses the mean of each
individual tree’s prediction as the final output, and for the
classification task, the most frequently categorized variable will
yield the predicted class. In this case, the trees are smaller versions
of the Random Forest, and integrating a series of weaker learners
and combining their predictions enables better generalization to new,
unseen data.
Bayesian
optimization can calculate the conditional probabilities of newly
generated metamaterial structure, which relies on the Bayes’
law:
where Y, U, and X represent the metamaterial’s properties,
desired properties, and design parameters. p(X|Y ∈ U) denotes
the probability to generate designed structure under the desired requirement. p(Y ∈ U|X) indicates the appearing probability of properties given
a known design structure, which could be obtained by the structure–property
relationship through different approaches, e.g., the t-distribution linear regression model calculated by Ikebata et al.122 The prior distribution p(X) is the appearing probability of the metamaterial design
structure, aiming to reduce the occurrence of unfavorable structure.
According to Bayes law, as long as the p(X|Y ∈ U) and p(X) are obtained, the appearing probability
of structure under the target properties can be acquired for inverse
design problem.123
Bayesian optimization
is a representative adaptive (or active) learning method.124,125 The Bayesian framework has been reported to behave in a human-level
performance with less data. In contrast to the neural network method,
the Bayesian approach enables one to initialize training with a relatively
low number of data sets (between 10 and 100 data points). Next, a
structure–property mapping is constructed after a few iterations.
The model is applied to another set of unseen structures to discover
the optimal material closest to the targeted property. Finally, the
data set size is expanded by adding the predicted material-property
relation after the characterization of the sample generated through
experimental synthesis or simulation.126 As the data set expands, the model becomes more accurate. Hence,
Bayesian optimization is suitable for the problem when acquiring data
set cost much computational or experimental resources.127
PCA can be broken into several steps: First, standardize the range
of continuous raw variables to ensure each contributes equally to
the analysis. Second, compute the covariance matrix and check how
each variable of the input data set changes the mean; this helps to
understand the underlying correlations between variables. Third, compute
the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the covariance matrix to determine
the data set’s principal components; typically, the largest
principal component should account for the largest variance of the
original data set. Fourth, keep the principal components with larger
eigenvalues and build a matrix with columns as the eigenvectors of
the kept components; the formed matrix is also named feature vectors.
Finally, reorient the original data set along the principal axis to
obtain a final data set. Assisted by PCA, a collection of different
good designs represented by high dimensional parameters vector are
reduced to low dimensional principal components, with sparse original
designs characterized by continuum region in the subspace. This subspace
is responsible for revealing the interplay of design parameters and
inspiring new design protocols.
These machine learning models
have proven effective in predicting thermal transport properties,
such as thermal conductivity κ and interfacial thermal resistivity.
In a study by Wei et al.,68 supportive
vector regression, Gaussian process regression, and CNN models were
employed to predict the effective thermal conductivities of composite
materials. Given the diversity of machine learning algorithms, it
is crucial to assess their performance and choose the most suitable
one for a specific problem. Evaluation metrics like R and RMSE can be utilized for this purpose. To enhance the thermal
conductivity of uranium dioxide (UO2), Yan et al.128 proposed and experimentally verified that introducing
a 2% volume fraction of Mo into the UO2 matrix can increase
the thermal conductivity by approximately 20% compared to pure UO2. The analysis involved mapping results of four machine learning
algorithms: GBDT, SVR, GPR, and ANN. Seko et al.129 utilized Bayesian optimization to screen a library of 54 779
compounds and identified 221 materials with low lattice thermal conductivity.
Two materials with thermal conductivities of <0.5 W/mK at 300 K
were identified, showing promising potential for thermoelectric applications
with a high figure of merit. Wu et al.130 employed Least-Squares Boosting (LSBoost) to analyze a diverse set
of 2,025 interfaces. LSBoost demonstrated superior performance with
an R value and RMSE of 0.93 and 11.9 × 10–9 m2 K W–1, respectively,
outperforming other models such as SVM and Gaussian regression processes.
The predicted and synthesized Bi/Si nanocomposite exhibited the lowest
κ, achieving an impressive value of 0.16 Wm–1 K–1.
The selection of descriptors and the
most accurate machine learning
(ML) model must be approached delicately based on the specific problem
at hand. In their investigation of the top five important features
influencing thermal conductivity κ, Wang et al.131 found that XGBoost outperformed other models,
such as SVR, kernel ridge regression (KRR), and fully connected neural
networks, achieving an average mean absolute error of 2.13 Wm–1K–1. The study focused on predicting
thermal conductivity within the Inorganic Crystallographic Structure
Database (ICSD) and successfully identified materials with low κ,
such as BiTe2Tl and Cl2CsI, which were further
validated using first-principles calculations. Lortaraprasert et al.132 employed 10 different supervised machine learning
models, including KNN, RF, and various tree-based models like CatBoost
and GradientBoosting, to predict the thermal boundary conductance
of crystalline–crystalline and crystalline–amorphous
interfaces. Their findings highlighted that variations in interatomic
angles and distances at silicon grain boundaries were the most predictive
structural descriptors. Wu et al.133 discovered
ultralow thermal conductivity Bi/Si with 0.16 Wm–1 K–1, utilizing machine learning models LSBoost,
SVM, and GRP over 80 000 material systems. The descriptors
used for training were meticulously categorized into three sets: physical,
chemical, and materials properties. This categorization helped reduce
the mismatch between predicted and experimental values, achieving
a high prediction performance of 96%. Yang et al.134 reported that deep neural networks outperformed decision
tree and random forest models in predicting interfacial thermal resistance
between graphene and hexagonal boron-nitride. Foss et al.135 identified influential descriptors for predicting
thermal boundary conductance over a range of van der Waals materials
through sensitivity analysis using a trained random forest model.
Assisted by the random forest model, Carrete et al.136 screened three half-Heusler semiconductors with low thermal
conductivity below 5Wm–1 K–1 from
a pool of 79 000 entries in the AFLOWLIB.org database. They discovered that compounds with
a large average radius of atoms in structural positions A and B were
more likely to exhibit low thermal conductivities.
Machine learning
techniques have proven to be effective in analyzing high-dimensional
data sets and extracting essential features to approximate physical
responses. In parallel, traditional optimization algorithms, including
both gradient-based and gradient-free methods, have also achieved
notable success in metamaterial studies. Gradient-based optimization
algorithms offer advantages in simplifying the optimization problem
with a high degree of freedom in design variables, requiring only
a limited number of function evaluations. However, a common drawback
is their tendency to converge to local optima because they iteratively
move solutions based on gradient functions. Moreover, they are applicable
only when the gradient expression is relatively easy to derive. Additionally,
when the objective function cannot be formulated as convex, achieving
the global minimum becomes unlikely.137 In contrast, gradient-free algorithms rely on extensive iterative
computations to explore the entire solution space, aiming to find
the global optimum. These algorithms do not depend on gradient information
from the physical model, making them suitable for cases where gradient
information is either unavailable or unreliable for computing metamaterial
parameters. They update their parameters stochastically, either by
emulating biological/physical processes (e.g., genetic algorithms,
particle swarm optimization, and simulated annealing) or through probabilistic
methods to identify a global optimal solution. However, their stochastic
nature needs substantial computational resources and may not be well-suited
for optimizations involving extensive simulations for property characterization.
Although they are relatively easy to use, they require repeated tuning
of algorithm hyperparameters to achieve the global optimal solution.
To reduce computational burden, these algorithms are often combined
with discriminative networks, such as deep neural networks, which
act as surrogate models replacing the computationally extensive simulation
of metamaterial responses. Additionally, the effectiveness of these
black-box optimization algorithms depends on the dimensionality of
the solution space, specifically the degrees of freedom of the metamaterial.
When applying these gradient-free algorithms, researchers are advised
to select a small number of design parameters for optimization. This
precaution is due to the curse of dimensionality,138 which suggests that increasing the number of design parameters
can slow down the optimization process and decrease the likelihood
of finding a global optimal solution.139 To address this issue, dimensionality reduction techniques, such
as GAN, VAE, and other machine learning algorithms that can construct
a compressed design space, are efficient methods for optimization.
However, because these methods have different formulations and mechanisms,
optimizing the same problem using different algorithms does not guarantee
identical results. If researchers are able to achieve the same solution
through different optimization algorithms, then it could conclude
that the obtained result represents a global optimum.
The Genetic
Algorithm (GA) is inspired by natural selection, where the fittest
individuals have a higher chance of reproducing and passing on their
genes to the next generation through evolution.28 GA is a crucial method within the field of evolutionary
algorithms due to its simplicity, flexibility, and compatibility.
In GA optimization illustrated in Figure 14, a candidate solution within a multivariate
design space is represented by a string called a chromosome, which
consists of individual variables encoded as genes. Typically, numeric
values are converted into binary strings for encoding. In the context
of metamaterials optimization, each gene bit can represent a design
parameter, such as the width or length of a unit cell. A population
is formed by a variety of possible chromosomes, which can be randomly
initialized or intelligently generated based on the prior knowledge
of the design space. For each specific problem, an objective function
is defined to evaluate the performance of each chromosome and select
those with the best fitness values. Individuals in the initial population
are assigned fitness values based on the objective function. Individuals
with higher fitness values are more likely to be selected for reproduction.
After initialization, a new population with the same number of chromosomes
is created through three evolutionary operations: selection, crossover,
and mutation. Selection involves choosing individuals with the highest
fitness values in the current generation to proceed to the next iteration.
Crossover, or reproduction, involves combining sections of chromosomes
from selected individuals to generate new candidate solutions. Mutation,
on the other hand, perturbs randomly selected genes within a chromosome
to explore different regions of the design space. The occurrences
of crossover and mutation are determined by specified probability
rates, which are hyperparameters adjusted manually during the operation
process. Typically, a random number between 0 and 1 is generated,
and crossover or mutation is accepted if the generated number is smaller
than the probability rate. The crossover probability is typically
set to be relatively high, generally in the range of 0.7 to 1.0, because
a small crossover rate is not sufficient for evolution.140 In contrast, the mutation rate is often assigned
a very small value, usually in the range of 0.001 to 0.05, which is
less than 1% probability.141 This small
mutation rate helps prevent excessive “jumping around”
of solutions, particularly when the optimal solution is in close proximity.
A too-large mutation rate could lead to erratic jumps, hindering the
convergence of the algorithm to the optimal solution. By combining
crossover and mutation, offspring with superior performance to their
parent can be stochastically generated, preventing the search from
becoming trapped in local optima within the solution space. The algorithm
terminates if the produced offspring are not significantly different
from their parents. Throughout the workflow, the population size remains
constant by replacing individuals with lower fitness scores with new
offspring.

Genetic algorithm workflow and basic concepts.
The GA offers advantages over gradient-based optimization
techniques
as it does not rely on gradient information, making it more accessible
and easier to be employed for a wide range of researchers. Consequently,
GA has gained popularity and is increasingly attractive. However,
it is important to carefully tune the hyperparameters of GA, such
as the crossover rate and mutation rate, as they greatly influence
the efficiency and convergence of an optimization problem. The optimal
values of these hyperparameters vary depending on the specific optimization
situation, and there are no standardized metrics or rules to determine
their appropriate values. Therefore, it is crucial to dedicate effort
to fine-tuning these hyperparameters. Furthermore, the fitness function
used in GA needs evaluation through simulation methods, which can
be computationally expensive. To reduce the number of required simulation
verifications and allow more emphasis on hyperparameter tuning for
achieving optimal performance, it is possible to substitute simulations
with deterministic machine learning models.
Certainly, determining
the optimal combination of hyperparameters
a priori poses a challenge. A straightforward grid search can be employed
to find suitable hyperparameters, as taken by Kerr et al.142 in maximizing the thermal conductance of a
one-dimensional classical harmonic oscillator using genetic algorithms
and simulated annealing. However, gaining insights into the underlying
mechanisms and fundamental principles of these optimization algorithms
may offer guidance in selecting hyperparameters and, importantly,
contribute to saving computational time and effort.
Several
widely adopted implementations of the crossover operation
exist. In one-point crossover, a random position within the parent
chromosomes is selected, and the corresponding subparts are exchanged.
This strategy is commonly used in practice. The multipoint crossover
operator divides the chromosomes into multiple segments, and the segments
are swapped between the two parents. The segment crossover is a variant
of multipoint crossover, where the number of crossover points varies
across generations. In uniform crossover, every gene is eligible for
exchange between the parents. Termination criteria should be carefully
designed. Typically, there are three termination strategies: reaching
an optimal solution, processing a certain number of generations, and
processing a certain number of generations after the solution has
not changed or improved significantly. However, identifying the optimal
solution may be impractical or impossible.
Additional considerations
involve the selection of mutation sites
and the adoption of diverse population sizes. Single-site mutation
is often inefficient; introducing mutations at multiple sites enhances
evolutionary efficiency. However, an excessive number of mutants can
impede system convergence or, in extreme cases, lead the system astray
toward incorrect solutions. In real ecological systems, a high mutation
rate under intense selection pressure may result in the extinction
of the entire population. Furthermore, the selection of an appropriate
population size is crucial. If the population size is too small, there
may be insufficient evolution, posing a risk of population extinction.
In a small population, the emergence of a significantly more fit individual
early on may lead to the reproduction of enough offspring to overwhelm
the entire small population. This could ultimately drive the system
toward a local optimum rather than the global optimum. Conversely,
if the population is too large, additional evaluations of the objective
function are required, demanding extensive computing time. Some typical
values of the population size and the genome length range from 50
to 1000.143
Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) is a stochastic evolutionary strategy
that takes inspiration from the social behavior of animal species
searching for desired items within a search area. It emulates the
behavior of a flock of birds, with each bird represented as a particle
searching for food. The particles share information with the entire
swarm, similar to how birds communicate and share knowledge within
a flock. PSO has gained significant interest from researchers due
to its convenience and promising optimization capabilities. In PSO,
each individual particle moves collectively through the design space
with a specific velocity. With multiple iterations, the positions
of the particles gradually converge toward the optimal point, as shown
in Figure 15.

and concept of particle swarm optimization.

plane, and t is the iteration step. Initially, a
set of particles are randomly generated. Each particle’s position
is updated through a velocity parameter Vi (t) = (vix(t),viy(t)) as:

Note that pibest,x and pibest,y record the optimal value of f discovered
by particle i while gbest,x and gbest,y are the best explored values across the entire swarm.
Parameter ω is introduced as the inertia weight constant, which
determines the extent to which a particle retains its previous velocity.
In the simplest case, the inertia term is a constant within the range
0.5–0.9. While there are many variants that modifies the standard
PSO algorithm which uses the inertia function ω(t), where ω(t) takes the values between 0 and
1 in theory.144,145r1 and r2 are random numbers ranging from
0 to 1. c1 and c2 are defined as the cognitive and social coefficients, respectively,
controlling the importance of individual particle information and
swarm information in updating the particle’s velocity. The
new velocity of a particle is influenced by its previous velocity,
best personal position (pibest), and the best swarm
position (gbest). The best
position of ith particle pibest is updated if the current performance of the particle is better
than its previous best position, and the best swarm position gbest is updated if the ith
particle’s performance at the current state surpasses the best
performance of the swarm as a whole. Δt is
the time step which typically set as 1. The initial positions of particles
should be distributed uniformly over the solution space so that they
can sample most regions. Each particle continues to search iteratively
until its best solution matches the best solution found by the entire
swarm. The primary mechanism of PSO lies in the cooperation and competition
among the members of the social swarm, which allows for a greater
chance of finding global optima based on collective memory rather
than relying solely on a single particle’s random search.
PSO can also be extended to optimize problems in a multidimensional
space. In this case, the dimensionality of the position vector Xi (t) is increased from two dimensions to N dimensions,
corresponding to an N-dimensional search space. Each
particle in the swarm is now represented by a point in this high-dimensional
space. In this case, the position of particle i is
represented by an N-parameter vector Xi (t) = (xi1(t),xi2(t), . . .,xiN(t)), and its velocity is also represented by a
multidimensional vector Vi (t)=(vi1(t),vi2(t),
. . .,viN(t)).
The particles’ position vectors Xi (t) in a swarm encode
the design parameters of a metamaterial configuration. After evaluation
among all particles in the initial swarm, the best previous particle
position Pibest is set as Pibest = (pi1,pi2, . . .,piN), and the position
of the best-performed particle in the swarm is set as Gbest. The modification of particle’s
position in the next round iteration is expressed as:
PSO offers the advantage of easy implementation,
few hyperparameters
to be tuned, and faster convergence. It has been successfully applied
in multiobjective optimization scenarios.146−148 As the algorithm operates at the particle level, careful attention
should be given to tuning both behaviors of individual particle and
the entire swarm. A complete iteration corresponds to the position
update of each individual particle. However, researchers can adopt
predetermined rules for choosing particles to increase the likelihood
of obtaining globally optimal solutions. For instance, particles with
better performance can be updated more frequently than others.149 Alternatively, researchers may focus on improving
the performance of poorly behaved particles to enhance the overall
group performance. However, in certain situations, it may be beneficial
to ignore outliers, particles that move to regions far from the main
swarm or even outside the parameter search space, and cease evaluating
these particles. For such cases, researchers may choose to relocate
or reinitialize these outlier particles in the next iteration. Each
strategy is feasible for specific scenarios and problems, and researchers
are encouraged to experiment with these methods in their studies to
determine the most effective approach.
Simulated
Annealing is named after physical annealing process, in which a solid
is heated to a high temperature then gradually cooling down until
crystallization, obtaining the lowest energy state.150 It is a suitable method searching for global minima for
an optimization problem, as shown in Figure 16a. The key mechanism of simulated annealing
is that it can jump out of local minima by accepting worse solutions
probabilistically, also referred as Metropolis criterion. Consider
an objective function f(xi(t)), corresponding to parameters
set (x1(t),x2 (t), . . .xN(t)) at a certain time point t optimizing
to a global minimum. If f(xi(t + 1)) < f(xi(t)), then take xi(t + 1) as a new candidate of extreme point. However, if f(xi(t + 1)) > f(xi(t)), then the candidate xi(t + 1) could
be accepted at a probability P = exp(−(f(xi(t + 1)) – f(xi(t)))/Tt), where Tt is the current temperature. A random number s is generated with 0 < s < 1, and
if s < P is true, the candidate xi(t + 1) is
also accepted otherwise rejected and system returns to search another
candidate. After enough iterations, system converges to the global
minima. The peudocode of SA algorithm has been summarized in Figure 16b.

(a) Schematic diagram
of the Simulated Annealing, illustrating
its ability jumping out of local optimal solution and find the global
optima. (b) Pseudocode of the Simulated Annealing algorithm.
The selection of the initial temperature T is
of paramount importance in simulated annealing. For a given change
in the objective function (Δf), an excessively
high temperature (in the extreme case, T →
∞) leads to P → 1, indicating that
almost all changes will be accepted. Conversely, if T is too low (approaching T → 0), worse solutions
are rarely accepted, limiting diversity, and only decrease in Δf are considered. In essence, an extremely high T corresponds to a system in a high-energy state on the
topological landscape, making it challenging to reach minima. Conversely,
an excessively low T may trap the system in a local
minimum, lacking the energy to escape and explore other minima, including
the global minimum. Thus, determining an appropriate initial temperature
is crucial for effective simulated annealing.
On the other hand,
under a given annealing temperature, a sufficient
number of evaluations is necessary. Insufficient evaluations may prevent
the system from stabilizing and reaching global optima. Conversely,
excessive evaluations prolong computation time and postpone the convergence
process. The computational resources required for iterations to achieve
stability are proportional to the problem size itself. Two commonly
used annealing schedules are linear cooling and geometric cooling.
In the linear cooling schedule, Tt = T0 – βt, where T0 is the initial temperature,
and β is the cooling rate. In the geometric cooling schedule,
the temperature is reduced by Tt = αT0, where α is
typically chosen as α = 0.9–0.99.
Topological
optimization is highly versatile in structural design, as it not only
alters the shape but also generates new pores throughout the optimization
process.151 It is characterized by the
allocation of material, whether existing or not, at specific points
within a defined area to fulfill an objective function. In this approach,
each grid point serves as a design parameter, resulting in the optimization
of geometry in a pixel-like fashion. Given that design variables introduced
in topology optimization can represent diverse shapes and topologies
for the design target, topology optimization methods have the potential
to produce superior designs. Numerous topology optimization methods
have been proposed because the pioneering work by Kikuch.152
Various structural expressions employed
in topology optimizations include the homogenization method,152,153 density method,154,155 and level-set method.156,157 The first two methods find widespread applications in the design
of high-performance optical devices. These approaches yield optimal
configurations that involve intermediate materials between dielectrics
and air, often referred to as grayscales.158 The presence of these grayscales can pose challenges in the fabrication
of optimally designed configurations. To address this issue, discrete
filtering schemes have been proposed to eliminate grayscales from
the design configurations.159,160 Another approach to
overcome the grayscale issue is a level-set method. The level-set
method creates configurations by utilizing two distinct phases defined
by a scalar function known as the level-set function. This method
facilitates discrete topology during optimization. The level-set function
assumes a positive value within the configuration, a negative value
outside the configuration, and a zero value at the boundaries of the
configuration.161−163 Topological optimization has been applied
in designing thermal cloak,164−167 concentrator,168,169 rotator,170 and camouflage.171 We are not ambitious to present a review covering
each point of topological optimization, as the main storyline of this
review is thermal metamaterials and machine learning. For more detailed
information, readers are recommended to read several references.172−176
Given a set of design
parameters x of a material, we could
define a cost function f(x,y) to represent the performance
or a material’s response. The adjoint method aims to optimize
the set of design parameters x by computing
the gradient ∇xf of the cost function to minimize the cost function f with the constraint of governing equation g(x,y)
= 0. To do so, the transposition of the Jacobian matrix gTy is used. For electromagnetic materials, g could be the Maxwell’s equations while y represents the electromagnetic fields. This method
requires iterative computation of f and its gradient
during the optimization process. It is an efficient technique which
often requires profound knowledge and expertise of the physics involved.
Some commonly used machine learning and optimization algorithms
are shown in Table 1.
In 2008, Fan et al.184 and Chen et al.185 extended transformation optics from wave systems to heat conduction
in steady state, a concept referred to as transformation thermotics.
This extension was possible because time-independent wave equations
share the same form as time-independent heat conduction equations.
Guided by transformation thermotics, they successfully achieved thermal
cloaking and apparently negative thermal conductivities. Taking a
step forward, Narayana et al.186 conducted
the pioneering experiment in thermal metamaterials. Employing multilayered
structures rooted in the effective medium theory, they successfully
fabricated three distinct devices endowed with cloaking, concentrating,
and rotating functionalities. The above works discussed steady cases
of heat conduction, leaving transient cases untouched. Schittny et
al.187 incorporated the time-dependent
parameters, specifically temperature, to design thermal cloaking for
transient cases. Employing multilayered structures as before, they
strategically drilled holes of varying sizes in each layer to match
the anticipated parameters.
The transformation theory can be
extended to heat sources, giving rise to the thermal illusion.188 Thermal illusion is an effect wherein the temperature
field surrounding a heat source undergoes modification, rendering
a measurement of the altered field incapable of revealing the true
shape, size, or number of the heat sources. This effect is achieved
through the transformation of the region occupied by the heat source
into other shapes. By manipulating the heat conduction near the surface
of an object, one can effectively modify the radiative signal. This
concept has been put into practice through the fabrication of a structured
thermal surface designed for radiative camouflage.189 Transformation thermotics typically demands anisotropy,
inhomogeneity, and singularity in thermal conductivity, introducing
manufacturing challenges. Addressing this, a bilayer structure has
been theoretically proposed and experimentally verified for cloaking
heat flux.190 Notably, this approach achieves
cloaking using isotropic materials instead of relying on extreme parameter
conditions.
Transformation heat transfer has been thus far centered
around
linear thermal conductivities, indicating that these conductivities
are temperature independent. However, many natural materials, such
as glasses and ceramics, exhibit nonlinear characteristics with temperature-dependent
thermal conductivities. This raises the crucial question of whether
existing transformation heat transfer can be extended to accommodate
nonlinear cases. Addressing this challenge, Li et al.191 proposed the theory of temperature-dependent
transformation heat transfer. In their experimental setup, shape-memory
alloys were employed to introduce nonlinear thermal conductivity.
The resulting composites exhibited the behavior of a thermal diode,
marking a pioneering exploration into the realm of nonlinear thermotics
and intelligent thermal metamaterials. While thermal cloaking can
maintain the central region at a constant temperature under fixed
boundary conditions, this temperature may vary if the boundary conditions
change. Recognizing this limitation, Shen et al.192 introduced a thermostat through the application of two
types of shape-memory alloys, ensuring the temperature of the central
region remains unchanged. Significantly, this thermostat operates
without requiring additional energy input, earning it the designation
of a zero-energy-consumption thermostat.
Convection stands as
a fundamental mechanism of heat transfer,
particularly dominant in mobile media like fluids. Convection denotes
the heat transport driven by the movement of the medium, specifically
through advection. It commonly coexists with other mechanisms, notably
conduction. The prevalent governing equation for heat transfer in
moving media is the widely recognized convection–diffusion
equation. Notably, convective systems exhibit considerably higher
heat dissipation efficiency compared to conductive counterparts. The
increased heat dissipation in convection arises from the proportional
relationship between convective heat flux and velocity, potentially
achieving an infinite effective conductivity. Hence, convection introduces
novel phenomena to the design of thermal devices with functionalities
beyond the scope of conduction alone. Building upon this concept,
Li et al.193 demonstrated that a thermal
zero-index implies an infinite thermal conductivity. They ingeniously
designed a bilayer structure to shield an object, showcasing the transformative
potential of leveraging convection for advanced thermal applications.
Convective systems can also be composed solely of solid components,
provided that at least one component is in motion or deformed. When
the convective term competes with the diffusive nature of conduction,
intriguing phenomena can emerge. A recent investigation unveiled a
breakthrough in the context of a diffusion heat transfer system, featuring
two coupled solid rings rotating at equal-but-opposite speeds.194 The study revealed the breaking of antiparity–time
symmetry when the rotation speed exceeded the exceptional point. This
novel finding expands our understanding of quantum-inspired phenomena
in diffusion systems with potential applications in various fields.
Thermal radiation stands as another significant mode of heat transfer,
as any object with a nonzero temperature emits thermal radiation.
Consequently, akin to thermal convection, thermal radiation typically
occurs in conjunction with thermal conduction. The concurrent manipulation
of thermal conduction and radiation represents a dynamic and actively
explored area within metamaterial research. Recently, Xu et al.195 introduced the theory of transformation multithermotics
to simultaneously control thermal radiation and conduction. This novel
approach opens avenues for designing thermal cloaks, concentrators,
and rotators. Radiating thermal metamaterials find application in
diverse areas, including thermal imaging. For instance, Li et al.189 achieved thermal radiative camouflage through
transformation thermotics. Furthermore, radiative cooling, a common
occurrence in daily life, gains added significance. Metamaterials
also hold the potential to achieve radiative cooling, particularly
suitable for further applications such as comfortable clothing.196−198
For more detailed information, please refer to some comprehensive
reviews.199−201
Heat transfer, a common occurrence
in our daily lives, refers to
the exchange of thermal energy between physical objects. This phenomenon
can be categorized into different mechanisms, including thermal conduction,
thermal radiation, and thermal convection. Thermal metamaterials,
deliberately crafted structures, exhibit exceptional heat transfer
properties that surpass those of naturally occurring materials. Delving
into the foundational theories of thermal conduction, researchers
such as Wang et al.202 organized them into
two distinct categories: the macroscopic phenomenological theory and
the microscopic phononic/thermal photonic theory. The former draws
upon the principles of transform heat transfer and its extensions,
while the latter is intricately linked to the domains of phononics
and photonics. Consequently, the utilization of thermal metamaterials
empowers the manipulation of thermal conduction within solids, employing
both macroscopic and microscopic strategies. Notably, these strategies
have seen synergistic development in conjunction with machine learning,
as visually depicted in Figure 17. Leveraging the insights from transformation thermotics,
a range of functional thermal metamaterials has been conceived, encompassing
thermal cloaks, concentrators, and rotators, all of which serve as
pivotal components in effective thermal management approaches. Furthermore,
thermal radiation can be systematically influenced through ingeniously
designed structures. The versatile realm of machine learning has found
applications in two primary areas: the thermophotovoltaic (TPV) system
and radiative cooling. Machine learning techniques have also demonstrated
their efficacy in refining radiative performance of metamaterials.

Schematic
presentation of the thermal metamaterials that machine
learning has been used.
The
thermal conductivities κ of conventional materials typically
exhibit uniformity and isotropy, ranging from 0.03 Wm–1 K–1 (e.g., air) to 400 Wm–1 K–1 (e.g., copper). Various theoretical analyses and
simulation tools,203−205 including first-principles calculations,
Boltzmann transport equations (BTE), nonequilibrium Green’s
function (NEGF) theory, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, provide
reliable predictions of thermal conductivity and offer valuable insights
into the underlying thermal transport mechanisms. Natural materials
generally demonstrate isotropic thermal conductivity, where κ
is a constant. However, in single-crystalline materials, anisotropy
may arise due to the intrinsic orientation of the lattice, as is seen
in graphite. According to the Onsager reciprocity theorem,206 anisotropic thermal conductivity is described
by a symmetric tensor. Engineering anisotropy can be artificially
achieved in composite patterns, forming what is known as thermal metamaterials.
Similar to the mathematics of transformation Maxwell equation,207−213 researchers have explored the application of manipulating the Fourier
heat equation through transformation theory, a field known as transformation
thermotics.184,214 The manipulation of heat conduction
using transformation theory has garnered significant attention, enabling
the artificial manipulation of heat flux and the development of versatile
devices for diverse applications.215−217
Heat conduction typically occurs in solids and is governed by Fourier’s
law q = −κ·∇T, where q is the heat flux density, T describes the temperature fields as a function of space and time,
κ is the rank-two thermal conductivity tensor that plays a key
role in designing thermal metamaterials. The heat flux is transmitted
from a higher temperature region to a lower temperature region. Transformation
theory has been applied in manipulating macroscopic heat conduction
due to the form invariance of heat conduction equation in both steady
states184,185 and transient states.218 The basic insight is that the heat transfer in the real
space r can be described as if propagating in the
virtual space r’. Taking into account energy
conservation, the temperature field describing a region without an

to replicate it. The most commonly investigated transformation is
the cloaking transformation, which dilates a point into a finite volume
(r ∈ (0,b) → r′ ∈ (a,b), 0 < a < b):
where a is the radius of
